newsitem.title: GERMANY: German investors eye telecoms interests.
newsitem.headline: German investors eye telecoms interests.

text.p: With Germany's industrial blue chips queueing up to compete with soon-to-be-floated Deutsche Telekom, investors are being forced to look carefully for their best opportunities, analysts said on Thursday.
Utilities RWE, Veba AG and Viag as well as metals group Thyssen AG and engineering group Mannesmann AG are among the big names lining up for their slice of the German telecoms pie.
Investors tracking the DAX index of German shares will almost certainly buy Deutsche Telekom shares when the flotation exercise begins next month.
Telekom will account for five percent of the weighting of the DAX when it is floated and investors tracking the index need to stay neutral on their holdings in German shares.
However, many investors are now examining the competition more closely to see how they stand up.

RWE, the second biggest by market capitalisation of the three utilities, on Wednesday pulled out of its partnership with Bavaria's Viag, the smallest of the big three, and British telecoms giant British Telecom.
RWE is now to join with Veba, the largest of the German utilities by market capitalisation and second-largest in Europe, in its partnership with Britain's Cable & Wireless.
"I like Veba very much. The new alliance with Cable & Wireless and RWE could become an alliance with a global impact," said Karim Serrar, portfolio manager with fund managers Ceros in Frankfurt.
Serrar said Deutsche Telekom was unlikely to be able to reduce costs significantly and reckoned that Veba was better-placed to provide returns because of sensible alliances.
From a strategic investment point of view, many fund managers will already have invested in Veba and Mannesmann, Serrar said.
One problem with Veba is that the share is expensive, but this is not a problem with Mannesmann, which Serrar recommended.

"The company has reformed itself from a steel pipe manufacturer to a growth stock. It's no longer just a cyclical steel company and its telecoms profits have beaten expectations so far -- quite impressive," said Serrar.
Serrar also likes Viag, but not as a telecom stock.
"It's got deep pockets, good management but it's a conglomerate and doesn't have Veba's clear strategy on telecoms," said Serrar.
Some analysts said it difficult to strip out the revenues from telecoms in the different utilities, but that telecoms was becoming increasingly important to the way utilities are perceived.

"As far as revenues go, it's in the future that the telecoms businesses of these companies become relevant. But the stocks have run up on telecoms-related news before," said one Frankfurt-based telecoms analyst.
Telecommunications is just one of the areas into which German utility companies have diversified in recent years.

The effectively competition-free areas of power production and supply have long been cash cows, allowing utilities to diversify into areas like chemicals, logistics, mining and waste management, as well as telecommunications.
Of the three biggest utilities, analysts said that Veba was the closest to success in diversifying into telecoms.

"Veba wants to shift from the utilities cash cow to telecommunications -- the cash cow of the future. Energy profits are slowly being eroded, but by the year 2000 and beyond, Veba's future could be telecoms," said Serrar.
